To sound it, tap the wrist of the holding hand with the other fist, keeping the ring even without touching the bells directly. For a continuous ring, shake the instrument, but keep the metal bells pointing down. The point for beginners is to avoid the child's way of playing, raising it high with the bells facing up. The principle of sound is a metal shell, spherical or nearly so, containing a metal ball or a metal plate; the two strike each other and the sound comes out through an opening. 雪橇鈴具有明亮清脆的音色質感，帶有銀鈴般的璀璨光澤。其音域屬於高頻範圍，單個鈴鐺: Sleigh bells have a bright, crisp timbre with the glittering sheen of silver bells. Their range lies in the high frequencies; a single bell is quiet, but when many bells ring at once they produce a rich, layered sound. Because the sound is idiophonic, coming straight from the resonance of the metal itself and not amplified by a soundbox, it is natural and pure. Against the depth and precision of the metallophone, sleigh bells are lighter and more animated; against the triangle, their timbre is warmer and fuller, with a festive, homely atmosphere. When a large set of bells comes together the sound spreads into a continuous texture, the maker of a merry winter mood.
雪橇鈴常見於敲擊樂與民間舞蹈伴奏，如莫里斯舞，也用於聖誕裝飾、兒童音樂訓練及管絃: Sleigh bells are common in percussion and as an accompaniment to folk dance such as Morris dancing; they are also used in Christmas decorations, children's music training and orchestral scoring, and professional orchestras mostly use the straight-handled type. In the classical repertoire they appear in Mahler's Symphony No. 4, Prokofiev's Lieutenant Kijé Suite, Mozart's K. 605 German Dances and Carl Orff's Carmina Burana; in Christmas songs they serve as a rhythm instrument, standing for the bells of the sleigh deer.
雪橇鈴由歐洲克羅塔爾鈴發展而來，早期繫於馬具或牲口，用於馬車與雪橇，使行進時發出: Sleigh bells developed from the European crotal bell. Early on they were tied to harness or to livestock and used on carriages and sleighs, so that a moving vehicle made a ringing sound that warned pedestrians or announced the approach of someone important; this was necessary above all because a sleigh on packed snow is almost silent. They later entered folk dance, secular music and orchestral scoring — Mahler's Symphony No. 4 (1901) and Prokofiev's Lieutenant Kijé Suite (1934) both use them. Professional orchestras moved to the straight-handled type and children use a ring carrying several bells; Massachusetts law also requires bells on carriage sleighs.

The body is usually spherical, made from bent metal plate or from two halves riveted together, holding metal balls, short rods or glass marbles, with holes in the surface to let the sound out. To play them you tie the bells to a wooden stick or a ring, hold the grip in one hand and tap the wrist with the other, or shake them for a continuous ring.

Sleigh bells (Sleigh Bells, also called horse bells, cluster bells or snow bells) are an idiophone, Hornbostel–Sachs number 112.1, found in Europe, Asia, Africa, Latin America and elsewhere. The body is usually spherical, made from bent metal plate or from two halves riveted together, holding metal balls, short rods or glass marbles, with holes in the surface to let the sound out. To play them you tie the bells to a wooden stick or a ring, hold the grip in one hand and tap the wrist with the other, or shake them for a continuous ring. They were once used on carriages, sleighs and livestock, and they also appear in folk dance, orchestral music, ensemble music, Christmas songs and early-childhood music education.
